To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
post‐transplante weight gain is an independent risk factor for graft loss.
post‐transplanted patients with a weight gain of more than 10% during the first year had a higher risk of losing their graft.
post‐transplanted weight gain significantly reduced graft survival.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the risk of obesity on the graft survival of renal transplantation recipients.
the risk factors of graft loss in RTRs.
the impact of metabolic syndrome and obesity on renal transplant outcomes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
post‐transplanted weight gain is a risk factor for graft loss, but not MS per se.
post‐transplanted RTRs should be advised to avoid excessive weight gain in the first year after transplantation, especially those with DGF and/or high proteinuria.
post‐transplanted patients with a BMI of 30 or higher, or with a weight gain of more than 2.7 kg, should be carefully monitored.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk of graft loss is increased in the presence of obesity and post‐transplanted weight gain.
post‐transplanted patients should be encouraged to lose weight and avoid the development of MS.
the risk of graft loss was increased in RTRs with post‐transplant BMI gain of more than 2.5 kg/m2.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the risk factors for graft failure are similar to those for cardiovascular events in the general population, with the exception of diabetes.
the risk for post‐transplant graft failure is increased by weight gain.
weight management should be a priority in the post‐transplant period.
